problems.title: Who does what
problems.statement: The CUDA toolchain: front end → NVVM IR → PTX → ptxas → SASS.

parts.prompt: Inlining and loop unrolling are mostly done…
options: by the GPU at run time

problems.solution: ptxas maps virtual registers to physical ones and schedules for the target. High-level optimisations (inlining, unrolling, constant folding) happen in the LLVM-based middle end; ptxas also unrolls and schedules.

problems.title: Why ship PTX
problems.statement: A program is built with SASS for sm_75 and PTX for compute_75.

parts.prompt: On an sm_86 GPU it runs…
options: the PTX, JIT-compiled by the driver for sm_86

parts.prompt: Built with sm_75 SASS only, no PTX, it runs on sm_86…
options: not at all: SASS isn't compatible across major versions

hints: SASS compatibility holds only within a major architecture version.
problems.solution: SASS is specific to an architecture family; PTX is the forward-compatible contract the driver can JIT. Ship PTX for the newest virtual architecture you support.

problems.title: A dependent chain
problems.statement: GWX model: one warp, one instruction per cycle, FMA latency 4, an instruction waits for its sources.

parts.prompt: Cycles to finish 10 FMAs, each using the previous result?

hints: Dependent: issue every 4 cycles. Independent: one per cycle.
problems.solution: (a) 40 cycles. (b) 13: the last issues at cycle 9 and completes 4 later. Independence is worth 3× at this latency.

problems.title: Load then use
problems.statement: One warp: a global load (400 cycles), then 5 FMAs, each depending on the previous (the first on the load).

parts.prompt: Fraction of cycles the warp issues something, in %?

problems.solution: (a) 420 cycles, (b) 1.4% issue utilisation: one warp alone is hopeless. Either other warps or more independent work must fill the 400 cycles.

problems.title: Reading an instruction mix
problems.statement: A loop body compiles to 12 instructions, 2 of them FFMA.

parts.prompt: Ceiling on the GW-1 if issue-bound, GFLOP/s?

problems.solution: 16.7% and 256 GFLOP/s. Counting instructions in the generated code gives the issue ceiling before any profiling.

problems.title: Constants and division

options: No: it isn't exactly equal for all x; it uses a correctly rounded division sequence
Yes: dividing by a power of two equals multiplying by its reciprocal exactly

hints: The reciprocal of 3 isn't representable exactly.
problems.solution: Replacing division by multiplication with a rounded reciprocal changes results, so it requires fast-math. For powers of two the reciprocal is exact, so the transformation is legal and done. Write the multiply yourself when you accept the rounding.

problems.title: Where does time go

parts.prompt: Cycles for one warp: ld.shared then a dependent FMA?
Independent FMAs needed to cover one ld.shared with one warp?

hints: Fill the 24-cycle wait with other instructions.
problems.solution: (a) 28. (b) The FMA can issue at cycle 24 at the earliest; 23 independent instructions in cycles 1–23 hide the latency completely. That's what register tiles provide (Part 4).

problems.title: Which stage
problems.solution: LLVM IR with NVIDIA conventions. That's why LLVM knowledge transfers directly to GPU compiler work (and why Triton, Julia and others can target PTX through LLVM's NVPTX back end).

problems.title: Hidden 64-bit math
problems.statement: A kernel indexes x[i * stride + j] with 32-bit int i, stride, j, and 64-bit pointers.

options: a widening multiply-add (IMAD.WIDE) or extra conversions to form the 64-bit address

problems.solution: The index must be sign-extended and scaled into a 64-bit address: IMAD.WIDE or I2L plus 64-bit adds. Cheap once, costly in a tight loop; strength reduction (pointer increments) removes it.

problems.title: Scheduling and encoding
problems.statement: Who decides instruction order and the control bits in SASS?
problems.solution: ptxas. GPUs have no out-of-order engine; the compiler's scheduling and its encoded stall counts and dependency barriers are what hide latency within a warp.
